buyer: Founder or general manager owns data decisions; no dedicated analytics sponsor.
Head of growth owns acquisition efficiency and reporting budget.
Head of e-commerce owns trading, conversion and merchandising decisions.
Operations or supply-chain lead owns stock and replenishment decisions.
Finance leader owns margin, cash and reconciliation decisions.
Data/IT leader owns governed access and the shared analytics platform.
operator: No dedicated analyst: functional staff investigate data alongside daily work.
Marketing specialist analyses spend, campaigns and acquisition cohorts.
Merchandiser analyses products, variants, pricing and conversion.
CRM specialist analyses repeat buying, segments and lifecycle campaigns.
Inventory planner analyses demand, availability and replenishment.
Finance analyst reconciles revenue, costs and contribution.
Customer-support lead investigates returns, cancellations and service issues.
steward: No dedicated data role; an operator manages exports and access.
External analyst or agency maintains reporting and data definitions.
Internal analyst owns models, joins and metric definitions.
Data engineer maintains pipelines, reliability and source contracts.
Platform/security team controls permissions, audit and governance.

marketing: Campaign reporting: combine spend and orders to see channel performance.
Acquisition diagnosis: investigate changes by campaign, creative and audience; correlation is not causation.
Cohort-quality analysis: compare later repeat purchases and margin by acquisition source.
Budget simulation: compare allocation scenarios using explicit response assumptions.
Experiment planning: recommend controlled tests; budget owners approve execution.
product: Product sales reporting: rank products and variants by units, revenue and returns.
Conversion-funnel analysis: find drop-off by product or journey when events are available.
Basket analysis: identify co-purchase patterns for bundle hypotheses.
Assortment analysis: assess demand, availability and margin across the catalogue.
Price/assortment simulation: compare scenarios with stated elasticity and substitution assumptions.
Merchandising experimentation: test approved changes and assess results.
crm: Repeat-purchase reporting: measure observed cohorts and purchase intervals.
Customer segmentation: group customers by permitted behavioural signals.
Lifecycle diagnosis: investigate where repeat purchase or engagement drops.
Retention prediction: estimate churn or next-order timing only with adequate history and validation.
Lifetime-value modelling: estimate future contribution with uncertainty and cost assumptions.
Intervention planning: prioritise consented lifecycle experiments for human approval.
inventory: Stock visibility: reconcile on-hand stock by SKU and location.
Stock movement reporting: track receipts, sales, returns and adjustments.
Inventory performance analysis: calculate sell-through, turnover and stock cover with agreed definitions.
Exception detection: identify low stock, ageing stock and overstocks.
Stockout diagnosis: distinguish demand changes from inaccurate stock or delayed replenishment.
Demand forecasting: estimate future SKU/location demand; validate history, seasonality and uncertainty.
Safety-stock planning: model buffers using variability, lead times and service-level goals.
Replenishment planning: suggest quantities and timing using forecasts, stock and order constraints.
Allocation simulation: compare transfers or channel allocation under stock and fulfilment constraints.
Approved replenishment review: planners approve supported actions and monitor forecast error and stock outcomes; no automatic orders assumed.
purchase: Purchase requirement reporting: consolidate stock needs and open purchase orders.
Supplier performance analysis: compare observed lead times, delivery reliability and costs.
Demand-linked purchase planning: translate demand into proposed orders using lead times and minimum quantities.
Sourcing scenario comparison: compare suppliers, order timing and cash constraints.
Purchase approval and tracking: buyers authorise orders and monitor delivery exceptions; integration must support execution.
finance: Revenue reconciliation: reconcile orders, refunds, fees and settlements.
Contribution analysis: combine actual costs with sales; show missing costs explicitly.
Customer payback analysis: compare acquisition spend with observed cohort contribution.
Working-capital planning: assess stock commitments and payment timing.
Financial scenario planning: model demand, margin and cash assumptions for finance review; not booked accounts.
support: Service reporting: count contact reasons, returns and cancellations from authorised records.
Issue classification: group recurring product, delivery and payment complaints.
Root-cause investigation: join service themes with orders and operational events.
Impact prioritisation: assess repeat contacts, refunds and retention associations.
Service improvement planning: propose reviewed tasks and experiments; no autonomous refunds or outreach.

store: Single commerce source with manual CSV exports; no continuous ingestion.
Commerce APIs supply orders, products and customer records with stable identifiers.
Multiple sales channels require shared product/order definitions and deduplication.
POS, marketplaces or wholesale sources add distinct returns and settlement models; verify connectors.
growth: Separate advertising and CRM exports, with manual reconciliation.
Advertising and order feeds joined for descriptive performance reporting.
CRM events joined with consented order history for cohort analysis.
Governed customer identity and activation interfaces; permissions and supported actions verified.
operations: Operational records in spreadsheets; stock and supplier history may be incomplete.
Inventory/WMS feeds expose stock, movements and locations.
ERP/procurement feeds expose purchase orders, suppliers, lead times and costs.
Finance and support systems provide settlements, costs and service context.
Write-back APIs with scoped permissions, approval and audit are required before any execution.
data: Spreadsheet reporting; no shared data model.
Central warehouse with defined metrics and governed joins.
Semantic layer and reviewed natural-language analysis.
Validated predictive models and scenario engines; not implied by an LLM alone.
Governed decision support with human approval, monitoring and traceable outputs.

commerce-scale: Limited workload: few sources and a small catalogue; page angle: analytics for lean e-commerce teams.
Growing workload: more orders, campaigns and SKUs; page angle: analytics for scaling e-commerce operations.
Catalogue complexity: many variants, intermittent demand or long-tail SKUs; page angle: inventory analytics for complex catalogues.
Location complexity: multiple warehouses or fulfilment locations; page angle: multi-location inventory analytics.
Channel complexity: online, marketplace, POS or wholesale feeds; page angle: omnichannel analytics.
Entity complexity: several brands, currencies or entities; page angle: multi-brand data analytics.
commerce-quality: Sparse or inconsistent records: prioritise reconciliation and reporting; forecasting may be unsuitable.
Reliable IDs and transaction history: joins and descriptive comparisons are feasible.
Complete cost, returns and stock records: margin and inventory diagnosis become feasible.
Long enough relevant history with lead times and demand context: evaluate predictive readiness; do not guarantee accuracy.
commerce-controls: Periodic batch refresh is adequate for planning decisions.
Daily freshness is needed for trading and campaign reviews.
Operational exceptions require a verified low-latency pipeline and monitoring.
Sensitive customer/financial data requires least-privilege access and clear retention rules.
Cross-brand or regional data requires explicit permission boundaries and agreed definitions.

triggers: Manual reconciliation delays routine business decisions.
Departments disagree because metrics or identifiers are inconsistent.
Campaign growth creates reporting work that current staff cannot sustain.
Repeated stockouts or excess stock prompt better demand and replenishment planning.
Poor visibility into contribution or cash creates pressure to connect costs and revenue.
Additional channels or brands make the existing reporting approach unreliable.
Existing dashboards explain what happened but cannot support the next decision.
AI initiatives are blocked by unreliable data, permissions or a lack of reviewed workflows.
